what: Build Check Part 1 (ROC Operations Manual §14.2A): every source the Source Register lists for a finding was reopened on 8 October 2026 and each recorded quotation looked for on its page. 'also_says' lists further sentences the checkers confirmed on the same pages.

checks.recorded: "Nearly all of Iowa is now in Zone 5, with the northern half in 5a and the southern half in 5b."
checks.page_wording: Nearly all of Iowa is now in Zone 5, with the northern half in 5a and the southern half in 5b.
checks.note: Sentence is exact, about Iowa only (Iowa State Extension, Iowa), dated 12 Dec 2023. It says nothing about a half-zone shift nationally or older maps circulating; the page says the new map is about one quarter-zone warmer in much of the US.

checks.recorded: "The maps are only guides."
checks.page_wording: However, the maps are only guides.
checks.note: Exact (page adds 'However,'). Generic caution only; page does not say zones measure winter cold only or leave out summer heat, snow cover or spring frost. Iowa-based, no place stated for the sentence, no roses.

checks.recorded: "Nearly all of Iowa is now in Zone 5"
checks.page_wording: Nearly all of Iowa is now in Zone 5, with the northern half in 5a and the southern half in 5b.
checks.note: Sentence is exact but is only an Iowa zone statement; the page does not mention roses or say that rose timing is given by state/county/society rather than zone. Place: Iowa.

checks.recorded: "Periodically, these averages will be exceeded, sometimes by a wide margin."
checks.page_wording: Periodically, these averages will be exceeded, sometimes by a wide margin.
checks.note: Exact. Supports the general idea that zone averages can be exceeded in a given year, but it is written for Iowa/US zone map, not Georgia, and not about roses or signals. Dated 12 Dec 2023.

contradictions: Page says the 2023 map is generally about one quarter-zone warmer throughout much of the US, not half a zone (conflicts with AF-3 wording).

checks.recorded: "Early spring (after removing overwinter materials, if applicable) is the best time to prune roses."
checks.page_wording: Early spring (after removing overwinter materials, if applicable) is the best time to prune roses.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa State Extension, written for Iowa. No month window is in this sentence and the page does not mention Minnesota or northern Midwest; the 'late March to mid-April in Iowa' on this page is stated for transplanting, not pruning.

checks.recorded: "in the spring, just as the new growth begins to emerge."
checks.page_wording: Apply an all-purpose garden fertilizer, such as 10-10-10, in the spring, just as the new growth begins to emerge.
checks.note: Exact fragment; Iowa, new-growth signal for first spring feed. No month given and no Minnesota or early-to-mid-May window.

checks.recorded: "additional fertilizer applications during the first bloom period and in mid to late July."
checks.page_wording: Modern roses, such as hybrid teas, grandifloras, and floribundas, benefit from additional fertilizer applications during the first bloom period and in mid to late July.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa, modern roses. Gives mid to late July as a later feed; the page gives no last-feed date and does not mention August.

checks.recorded: "as fall approaches, it's best to stop."
checks.page_wording: Deadheading is desirable during the summer to promote more blooms, but as fall approaches, it's best to stop.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa. Says stop as fall approaches, no month named, no August or September.

checks.recorded: "as soon as they are received or purchased from the nursery (late March or April)."
checks.page_wording: Dormant, bare-root roses should be planted in early spring before spring growth begins, as soon as they are received or purchased from the nursery (late March or April).
checks.note: Exact; Iowa. Gives late March or April only; mid-May is not on the page and Minnesota is not mentioned.

checks.recorded: "Container-grown roses can be planted from April through midsummer."
checks.page_wording: Container-grown roses can be planted from April through midsummer.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa. Supports April (Iowa) through midsummer; no 15 May Minnesota start on this page.

checks.recorded: "After the first killing frost, removal of fallen leaves and flower debris is beneficial."
checks.page_wording: After the first killing frost, removal of fallen leaves and flower debris is beneficial to help reduce disease recurrence.
checks.note: Exact fragment; Iowa. Ties leaf clear-up to the first killing frost; no month (mid-to-late October) is stated.

checks.recorded: "The process for preparing roses for winter starts in late fall (mid-November)."
checks.page_wording: The process for preparing roses for winter starts in late fall (mid-November).
checks.note: Exact; Iowa. Winter preparation starts mid-November; the page gives no mid-to-late September start for mounding.

contradictions: Pruning sentence on this page gives no months; Iowa window late March to mid-April appears only for transplanting.
No dormant spray, hardiness zone, frost-date or forsythia signals on the page; page says to refrain from other pruning in fall.

also_says.quote: Early spring (before the plant begins to leaf out) is the best time to transplant a rose. This is typically late March to mid-April in Iowa.
also_says.note: Moving a rose, late March to mid-April, Iowa (page confirmed twice).

also_says.quote: This is done once the ground thaws and harsh cold temperatures of winter have passed, but before the plants break bud.
also_says.note: Removing winter protection in spring, no month, Iowa; signal is ground thaw and passing of harsh cold.

also_says.quote: Refrain from pruning any other plant material in the fall - this task is best left for spring.
also_says.note: No fall pruning, Iowa, roses.

checks.recorded: "in late March to mid-April."
checks.page_wording: Gardeners should prune out the dead wood after the winter protection is removed from modern roses in late March to mid-April.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa State Extension, Iowa. Supports late March to mid-April for Iowa only; finding is national across all sources and 'December' and 'later in colder areas' are not on this page.

checks.recorded: "Gardeners should prune out the dead wood after the winter protection is removed from modern roses in late March to mid-April."
checks.page_wording: Gardeners should prune out the dead wood after the winter protection is removed from modern roses in late March to mid-April.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa, modern roses, pruning out winterkill after protection comes off, late March to mid-April. Supports the Iowa part; Minnesota and northern Midwest are not mentioned.

checks.recorded: "after the winter protection is removed from modern roses in late March to mid-April."
checks.page_wording: Gardeners should prune out the dead wood after the winter protection is removed from modern roses in late March to mid-April.
checks.note: Exact; Iowa. Gives late March to mid-April for removing protection; the 'or once the ground thaws' condition is not on this page (it is on the Rose Care by Season page).

contradictions: Page does not mention forsythia, bud signals or hardiness zones.

checks.recorded: "Mound wood mulch over crowns (12–18 inches) after second hard frost (28 degrees)."
checks.page_wording: Mound wood mulch over crowns (12-18 inches) after second hard frost (28 degrees).
checks.note: Exact (December). UGA Extension Cobb County, Georgia. Supports a frost signal for mounding; page has no bud-swell or forsythia signal and names no zone.

checks.recorded: "Prune roses that repeat bloom (remontant) until March 15th."
checks.page_wording: Prune roses that repeat bloom (remontant) until March 15th.
checks.note: Exact (March); page also says last week in February. Cobb County, Georgia, repeat-blooming roses only. Supports Cobb part; Nashville is not on the page; no zone stated.

checks.recorded: "Fertilize with ..." (listed under March)
checks.page_wording: Fertilize with E. B. Stone Rose and Flower Food.
checks.note: Exact fragment under March (product named). Cobb County, Georgia, March feed. The page also lists April feeding; Nashville not covered.

checks.recorded: "Fertilize with ... for Roses every other week." (listed under September)
checks.page_wording: Fertilize with Miracle-Gro for Roses every other week.
checks.note: Exact under September. Cobb County, Georgia, still feeding in September. Nashville claims (granular too late, stop in November) not on the page.

checks.recorded: "Stop deadheading. Remove diseased leaves" (listed under October)
checks.page_wording: Stop deadheading. Remove diseased leaves from plants and beds.
checks.note: Exact under October. Cobb County, Georgia. Supports stopping deadheading in October; Nashville November claim not on the page.

checks.recorded: "Remove diseased leaves from plants and beds." (listed under November)
checks.page_wording: Remove diseased leaves from plants and beds.
checks.note: Exact under November (the same line also appears in October, May and June). Cobb County, Georgia. Leaf removal is for diseased leaves in beds, listed October and November; 'to winter' not stated.

checks.recorded: "Spray dormant oil every other week." (listed under December)
checks.page_wording: Spray dormant oil every other week.
checks.note: Exact under December. Cobb County, Georgia. The page also lists Neem oil spray every other week in November, so Nov-Dec fits; February Nashville dormant oil is not on the page.

checks.recorded: "Mound wood mulch over crowns (12–18 inches) after second hard frost (28 degrees)."
checks.page_wording: Mound wood mulch over crowns (12-18 inches) after second hard frost (28 degrees).
checks.note: Exact, under December. Cobb County, Georgia. Page says 28 degrees, not 'two freezes below 28 F'; otherwise matches.

contradictions: Page also advises pruning one-time bloomers after bloom in June and secures canes/cuts long canes in December.
No zone, forsythia or planting/moving advice on the page.

also_says.quote: Prune roses that repeat bloom (remontant) during last week in February.
also_says.note: Main pruning, last week of February, Cobb County, Georgia.

also_says.quote: Prune one-time blooming roses after bloom.
also_says.note: June, Cobb County, Georgia, one-time bloomers.

checks.recorded: "Generally, we have 2 climates to work around."
checks.page_wording: Generally, we have 2 climates to work around.
checks.note: Exact (December). Orange County, California rose society: coastal vs inland climates within the county. Supports different timing within one area, but not 'several states'.

checks.recorded: "Pruning each bush back and removing all foliage forces the energy of growing back into the roots and canes." (listed under January)
checks.page_wording: Pruning each bush back and removing all foliage forces the energy of growing back into the roots and canes.
checks.note: Exact, under January. Orange County, California; pruning/defoliating in January to force dormancy. Does not give ten other states' months.

checks.recorded: "When there is 3 inches of new growth, then you should fertilize."
checks.page_wording: When there is 3 inches of new growth, then you should fertilize.
checks.note: Exact, under January. Orange County, California; first feed tied to 3 inches of new growth. Other states in the finding are not on the page.

checks.recorded: "October is the last month to feed your roses."
checks.page_wording: October is the last month to feed your roses.
checks.note: Exact, under October. Orange County, California; supports the Orange County October part only.

checks.recorded: "Stop deadheading and pull off old petals." (listed under November, December)
checks.page_wording: Stop deadheading and pull off old petals.
checks.note: Exact, under November and December. Orange County, California; supports the Orange County part only; Kansas City not on page.

checks.recorded: "Need a new rose? It's bare root rose season!" (listed under January)
checks.page_wording: Need a new rose? It's bare root rose season!
checks.note: Exact, under January. Orange County, California; supports bare-root in January only.

checks.recorded: "a dormant spray such as copper sulfate and/or horticulture oil." (listed under January, February)
checks.page_wording: Using a dormant spray such as copper sulfate and/or horticulture oil (page lacks leading 'a')
checks.note: Near, trivial difference. Under January; coastal California / Orange County. Types named: copper and horticultural oil. February timing not confirmed by this check; page does not say 'coastal' for this sentence.

contradictions: Page names no other states, so none of the other-state claims are on it.

also_says.quote: A light pruning will help bring them back to earth.
also_says.note: August, Orange County, California.

also_says.quote: It still is not too late to prune.
also_says.note: February, Orange County, California.

checks.recorded: "Prune Hybrid Teas, Floribundas and Grandifloras in late winter before growth begins."
checks.page_wording: Prune Hybrid Teas, Floribundas and Grandifloras in late winter before growth begins.
checks.note: Exact; UGA Extension, Georgia statewide. Says late winter with no months; this is a Georgia statement, not ten other states.

checks.recorded: "each month from March through September."
checks.page_wording: it is generally recommended to use three tablespoons per plant of 16-4-8 or 12-4-8 fertilizer each month from March through September.
checks.note: Near: page continues 'each month from March through September'. Georgia, without a soil test. Supports Georgia March start only; no other states on the page.

checks.recorded: "each month from March through September."
checks.page_wording: it is generally recommended to use three tablespoons per plant of 16-4-8 or 12-4-8 fertilizer each month from March through September.
checks.note: Same sentence. Georgia; implies feeding to September. Finding's examples (Missouri, Kansas City, Orange County, Florida) are not on the page.

checks.recorded: "Roses should be planted 5 to 6 feet apart in February."
checks.page_wording: Roses should be planted 5 to 6 feet apart in February.
checks.note: Exact, but it is about spacing and does not give a bare-root planting season; Georgia, February. Page does not distinguish bare-root.

contradictions: No mention of deadheading end, dormant spray, winter protection, moving roses, zones or weather signals.

also_says.quote: Prune climbing roses after the first flush of blooms fade.
also_says.note: Climbing roses, after first flush, Georgia statewide.

checks.recorded: "Roses are usually pruned twice a year–in October and again in mid-February."
checks.page_wording: Roses are usually pruned twice a year-in October and again in mid-February.
checks.note: Exact. Texas AgriLife Extension, Bexar County (San Antonio), Texas; column dated 2003. Gives October and mid-February for Bexar; no zone and nothing about the ten other places.

contradictions: Page does not say what the October pruning is and names no zone.

also_says.quote: The late winter pruning is the most severe, as this is the time to truly renew the plant for spring growth.
also_says.note: Mid-February pruning is the main one, Bexar County, Texas, 2003 column.

also_says.quote: Spring blooming climbing roses MUST NOT be pruned until after they the first bloom in spring.
also_says.note: Climbers, Bexar County, Texas.

checks.page_wording: In our zone #7, December through the first of February is the ideal time.
checks.note: Phrase is on the page, but it shows this Nashville rose society (Middle Tennessee, zone 7 stated) tying its months to a zone label; it does not show that sources give months for their own area rather than a zone. Context: moving an established rose, December to 1 February.
checks.recorded: "In our zone #7"

checks.page_wording: In our zone #7, December through the first of February is the ideal time.
checks.note: Page is Nashville Rose Society, Middle Tennessee, zone 7 stated; moving established roses December through the first of February. Page also requires roses to be dormant or going dormant; dated 9 Nov 2020.
checks.recorded: "In our zone #7, December through the first of February is the ideal time."

contradictions: Page frames the months as 'our zone #7' (a USDA zone) for a Middle Tennessee society, which sits against AF-6's claim that sources avoid zones.

also_says.quote: Roses need to be dormant or going dormant, not actively growing, when they are moved. Late winter to early spring is the best time.
also_says.note: Moving established rose; late winter to early spring; Nashville, Middle Tennessee, zone 7. Note it differs from the December-February sentence.

checks.page_wording: Once we have two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees apply winter protection.
checks.note: Under December heading; Nashville Rose Society, Middle Tennessee, no zone in sentence. Winter protection goes on after two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees (page says degrees, Fahrenheit assumed): a weather signal, not a fixed date.
checks.recorded: "Once we have two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees apply winter protection"

checks.page_wording: Clean up all diseased leaves from the rose beds then spray the beds well.
checks.note: Sits under December, Nashville Rose Society (Middle Tennessee). Supports clearing diseased leaves and spraying beds, but only in December; October is not on this page and the spray type is not named.
checks.recorded: "Clean up all diseased leaves from the rose beds then spray the beds well"

checks.page_wording: Spray with a dormant oil spray when temps are over 40 degrees for 24 hours
checks.note: Under February; Nashville, Middle Tennessee; spray type is dormant oil, triggered by temperatures over 40 degrees for 24 hours. Supports the Nashville February half only; the Cobb County November-December oil half is not on this page.
checks.recorded: "Spray with a dormant oil spray when temps are over 40 degrees for 24 hours"

checks.page_wording: Once we have two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees apply winter protection.
checks.note: Under December heading; Nashville, Middle Tennessee. Two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees matches the finding's 'two freezes below 28 F'; the words 'second hard frost' are not on the page.
checks.recorded: "Once we have two consecutive freezes below 28 degrees apply winter protection"

contradictions: Spray in the December clean-up line is not typed; dormant oil appears only under February, so AF-49's Nov-Dec oil spray is not supported here.

also_says.quote: If a rose needs to be moved, move it between now and the first of February.
also_says.note: Moving established rose; December section; Nashville, Middle Tennessee.

also_says.quote: Cut hybrid teas back to about three feet to keep the wind from rocking the rose.
also_says.note: Winter height-reduction cut, December; Nashville, Middle Tennessee; not the main pruning.

also_says.quote: Prune and feed David Austins and climbing roses.
also_says.note: February; Nashville, Middle Tennessee; David Austin and climbing roses only.

checks.page_wording: It is getting too late to feed granular fertilizers, but you may certainly feed liquids ... for a while yet.
checks.note: September, Nashville Rose Society, Middle Tennessee. Granular is nearly too late but liquids continue; the Cobb County half of the finding is not on this page. 'Stop all feeding' appears under November.
checks.recorded: "It is getting too late to feed granular fertilizers"

checks.page_wording: Continue to cut buds and blooms (sometimes we have them until Thanksgiving!)
checks.note: November heading, Nashville, Middle Tennessee. Supports Nashville cutting blooms into November; the Cobb County October stop is not on this page.
checks.recorded: "Continue to cut buds and blooms (sometimes we have them until Thanksgiving!)"

checks.page_wording: Clean up beds.
checks.note: Under November (October says 'Keep garden clean and free of debris'); Nashville, Middle Tennessee. Supports clearing beds in autumn, not diseased leaves specifically and not 'to winter'.
checks.recorded: "Clean up beds."

contradictions: Same September line says liquid feeds may continue for a while; granular feeding is only 'getting too late'. Page also says 'Fall is not the time to prune!' (November).

also_says.quote: Stop all feeding.
also_says.note: November; bush roses; Nashville, Middle Tennessee.

also_says.quote: Prepare roses for winter protection.
also_says.note: November; Nashville, Middle Tennessee.

also_says.quote: Fall is not the time to prune!
also_says.note: November; Nashville, Middle Tennessee.

checks.page_wording: Prune roses by the end of month
checks.note: Under March; Nashville Rose Society, Middle Tennessee, no zone stated. Supports the end of March only; late February and Cobb County, Georgia are not on this page.
checks.recorded: "Prune roses by the end of month" (listed under March)

checks.page_wording: Apply fertilizer on established bushes

checks.recorded: "Apply fertilizer on established bushes" (listed under April)

checks.page_wording: Plant bare root roses

checks.recorded: "Plant bare root roses" (listed under March)

also_says.quote: Complete pruning early in the month

also_says.quote: Do first spray after pruning
also_says.note: March; Nashville, Middle Tennessee; type of spray not named (fungicide/insecticide named on the pruning page).

checks.recorded: "On or about the third week of March (depending on the weather), uncover the roses very carefully"

contradictions: Page also says to prune roses back by about one-third in late fall to prevent cane breakage in winter wind, which is a separate light autumn trim, not the main pruning.

also_says.topic: Q1 main pruning timing and signal
also_says.quote: Repeat blooming roses such as floribunda and hybrid tea roses need a heavy annual pruning that is done in the spring, just as the buds break dormancy.
also_says.note: Main spring pruning; South Carolina (Clemson Extension); signal is bud break.

also_says.quote: In the late fall, prune roses back by about one-third of their height. This helps prevent breaking of canes in winter winds.
also_says.note: Late fall light trim; South Carolina; no month named.

checks.recorded: "Stop fertilizing your roses six weeks before your expected first frost date."
checks.page_wording: Stop fertilizing your roses six weeks before your expected first frost date.
checks.note: Supports the frost-date signal for the last feed only. Written for South Carolina by Clemson Extension; for roses generally. Bud swell, forsythia and hard freezes are not covered by this quotation.

checks.recorded: "fertilize when the plant first leafs out"
checks.page_wording: For best performance, fertilize when the plant first leafs out and repeat after each flush of bloom until six weeks before the earliest frost date for your area.
checks.note: First feed is tied to leaf-out (new growth), not a month. Clemson Extension, South Carolina; roses generally. Supports the 'tied to new growth' option of the finding; no month is given here.

checks.recorded: "Stop fertilizing your roses six weeks before your expected first frost date."
checks.page_wording: Stop fertilizing your roses six weeks before your expected first frost date.
checks.note: Exact. Clemson Extension, South Carolina; no month or frost date is given, only 'six weeks before expected first frost date'. Another sentence says 'earliest frost date for your area'.

checks.recorded: "You can plant bare root roses in late fall, late winter or early spring in South Carolina."
checks.page_wording: You can plant bare root roses in late fall, late winter or early spring in South Carolina.
checks.note: Bare-root planting seasons for South Carolina (stated on page); seasons, not months. Supports the South Carolina part of the finding only; the other five states are not on this page.

checks.recorded: "Container-grown plants can be planted later in the spring."
checks.page_wording: Container-grown plants can be planted later in the spring.
checks.note: Supports 'later in spring' for potted roses in South Carolina. The page attaches no last-frost condition and says nothing about planting through the growing season, so those parts are not supported.

also_says.quote: fertilize when the plant first leafs out and repeat after each flush of bloom until six weeks before the earliest frost date for your area.
also_says.note: Feeding start at leaf-out, repeat after each bloom flush; South Carolina; frost-date signal.

checks.recorded: "prune after new buds start to swell."
checks.page_wording: In spring carefully wash soil and/or pull the mulch back and prune after new buds start to swell.
checks.note: Supports the bud-swell signal for spring pruning, written for the northern Midwest (Minnesota and Wisconsin named; no single zone stated for the region). Forsythia, frost and hard-freeze signals are not in this quotation; the page gives no calendar months for pruning.

checks.recorded: "In spring carefully wash soil and/or pull the mulch back and prune after new buds start to swell."
checks.page_wording: In spring carefully wash soil and/or pull the mulch back and prune after new buds start to swell.
checks.note: Supports main pruning in spring after protection is pulled back, for the northern Midwest (Minnesota Tip growers). The page gives no months, so the late March to mid-April (Iowa) window is not supported here; the signal is bud swell.

checks.recorded: "Begin fertilizing in early to mid-May after new growth is evident."
checks.page_wording: Begin fertilizing in early to mid-May after new growth is evident.
checks.note: Supports early to mid-May plus new growth for the northern Midwest. The Iowa 'as new growth emerges' part is not on this page; the sentence ties the month to visible new growth.

checks.recorded: "Ending especially nitrogen fertilization in late-July."
checks.page_wording: Ending especially nitrogen fertilization in late-July.
checks.note: Supports late July as the end of (especially nitrogen) feeding in the northern Midwest. The finding's range to the end of August is not supported by this sentence; this is the earliest end of the range.

checks.recorded: "Discontinuing to deadhead spent blooms in September."
checks.page_wording: Discontinuing to deadhead spent blooms in September.
checks.note: Stop deadheading in September, northern Midwest (Minnesota/Wisconsin region). Matches the finding's 'in September' option; the page says nothing about August or 'as fall approaches'.

checks.recorded: "Plant as soon as soil is workable and plants are available."
checks.page_wording: Plant as soon as soil is workable and plants are available.
checks.note: Sits under Planting Roses, Bareroot Rose Plants, northern Midwest. It gives a soil condition (workable) but no months, so late March to mid-May is not supported by this page.

checks.recorded: "One can begin to mound up soil around the crowns of your tender bush roses in mid to late September."
checks.page_wording: One can begin to mound up soil around the crowns of your tender bush roses in mid to late September.
checks.note: Supports mounding beginning mid to late September, northern Midwest. The page does not use the word November; it says to add leaves after the ground has frozen. The mid-November end is not supported.

checks.recorded: "In the spring, reverse the process just after the ground has thawed."
checks.page_wording: In the spring, reverse the process just after the ground has thawed.
checks.note: Supports removal once the ground has thawed (Minnesota Tip, northern Midwest). No months are given on the page, so late March to mid-April is not supported here.

contradictions: No months are given for pruning, bare-root planting or removing protection; the page uses signals (buds swell, soil workable, ground thawed) instead of calendar dates.
No month for the dormant spray is given.

also_says.quote: Apply a mixed lime-sulfur and horticultural oil dormant spray if desired.
also_says.note: Dormant spray; type is lime-sulfur mixed with horticultural oil; under the Minnesota Tip section; no month; northern Midwest.

also_says.quote: After the ground has frozen cover with additional leaves to provide insulation.
also_says.note: Winter protection goes on after the ground has frozen; northern Midwest; no month.

also_says.quote: The classes of old garden roses that are typically hardy to Zone 4 include: Albas, Gallicas, Mosses, and Damasks.
also_says.note: Zones used for plant hardiness, not for timing; page does not tie timing to USDA zones.

checks.recorded: "situated in USDA plant hardiness zones 3, 4, and 5."
checks.page_wording: The American Rose Society's North Central District includes the states of Minnesota, Wisconsin and North and South Dakotas, situated in USDA plant hardiness zones 3, 4, and 5.
checks.note: Confirms the page is written for a rose-society district (North Central District: MN, WI, ND, SD) whose zones are 3 to 5. It shows the district is named and its zones noted, but the sentence itself gives no months; the timings elsewhere on the page are for the district, not for a single zone.

checks.recorded: "stopping nitrogen fertilizers and discontinuing deadheading after August will encourage the hardening off"
checks.page_wording: Stopping nitrogen fertilizers and discontinuing deadheading after August will encourage the hardening off, or maturing, of the canes.
checks.note: North Central District (MN, WI, ND, SD; zones 3-5). Gives the end of August as the point to stop nitrogen feeding, the late end of the finding's range; it concerns nitrogen only, not all feeding.

checks.recorded: "stopping nitrogen fertilizers and discontinuing deadheading after August will encourage the hardening off"
checks.page_wording: Stopping nitrogen fertilizers and discontinuing deadheading after August will encourage the hardening off, or maturing, of the canes.
checks.note: North Central District (MN, WI, ND, SD). Deadheading is stopped after August, which fits 'after August'. Reason given is hardening off of canes.

checks.recorded: "Roses are dormant sprayed in mid to late October at the time when you are doing general fall cleanup"
checks.page_wording: Roses are dormant sprayed in mid to late October at the time when you are doing general fall cleanup.
checks.note: North Central District. Fall cleanup is placed in mid to late October (as the time of the dormant spray) but fallen leaves are not named and the first-killing-frost option is not on the page.

checks.recorded: "Roses are dormant sprayed in mid to late October"
checks.page_wording: Roses are dormant sprayed in mid to late October at the time when you are doing general fall cleanup.
checks.note: Dormant spray in mid to late October, North Central District (MN, WI, ND, SD; zones 3-5). The page does not name the spray type.

checks.recorded: "As the temperatures drop in early November, a blanket of leaves 12″ – 18″ deep is added"
checks.page_wording: As the temperatures drop in early November, a blanket of leaves 12″ – 18″ deep is added.
checks.note: North Central District. Supports the November leaf covering (early November, as temperatures drop). The mid-to-late September start of mounding is not supported by this sentence or found elsewhere on this page.

checks.recorded: "Early in April the leaves are removed. By the middle of April, the rest of the process is reversed"
checks.page_wording: Early in April the leaves are removed. By the middle of April, the rest of the process is reversed.
checks.note: North Central District. Supports early to mid April for taking protection off. The page gives April, not late March, and does not mention ground thaw here.

contradictions: The page does not name a type of dormant spray.
It says nitrogen stops after August; other Band A sources (e.g. ZLESAK) end feeding in late July.

checks.recorded: "Otherwise, mid-April pruning is best"
checks.page_wording: Otherwise, mid-April pruning is best.
checks.note: Colorado State Extension, Colorado: mid-April is the main pruning time, for roses not cut back in November. Supports the mid-April, colder-area end only; not the December start or a national pattern.

checks.recorded: "When the night temperatures drop to 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days, mound soil over the rose crown"
checks.page_wording: When the night temperatures drop to 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days, mound soil over the rose crown.
checks.note: Colorado. Supports a weather signal (nights of 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days) for putting on winter protection. Does not show a signal for pruning, and no forsythia or bud swell is mentioned.

checks.recorded: "Otherwise, mid-April pruning is best"
checks.page_wording: Otherwise, mid-April pruning is best.
checks.note: Supports Colorado mid-April only (of the ten areas listed). The sentence is preceded by advice to cut tall roses back by one-third in November, which is a separate light autumn trim.

checks.recorded: "Around Thanksgiving, remove all leaves and debris from the ground"
checks.page_wording: Around Thanksgiving, remove all leaves and debris from the ground; this will help prevent the spread of some diseases!
checks.note: Fragment is the start of a longer sentence; difference is trivial. Supports Colorado clear-up around Thanksgiving only; the Kansas City 'after hard freezes' part is not on this page.

checks.recorded: "When the night temperatures drop to 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days, mound soil over the rose crown"
checks.page_wording: When the night temperatures drop to 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days, mound soil over the rose crown.
checks.note: Supports the Colorado half (nights of 20 degrees Fahrenheit for several days). The Kansas City 'several hard freezes' half is not on this page.

checks.recorded: "Mulch should be removed gradually in the spring after the danger of hard frost has passed"
checks.page_wording: Mulch should be removed gradually in the spring after the danger of hard frost has passed.
checks.note: Supports the Colorado 'after danger of hard frost' part. The mid-April (Kansas City) and Missouri parts are not on this page.

contradictions: The page recommends pruning tall plants by one-third in November (Colorado), so 'main pruning mid-April' applies only to roses not so treated, and November is a second pruning time.

also_says.quote: To prevent this, prune all tall plants by one-third of their height in November.
also_says.note: Light cutback of tall roses against snow and wind damage; Colorado; November.

also_says.quote: Use pine needles or boughs, leaves, rotted manure or shredded newspaper.
also_says.note: Material for winter mounding/mulch; Colorado; applied after nights reach 20 degrees Fahrenheit.

checks.recorded: "These Zones are based on the average annual extreme minimum temperature"
checks.page_wording: These Zones are based on the average annual extreme minimum temperature expressed in degrees Fahrenheit (°F) or Celsius (°C).
checks.note: Supports 'average annual extreme minimum temperature' for the US (national, no place stated). The page does not give the 10 degrees F zone width or 5 degrees F half zones (asked twice; not found), so that part is not supported.

checks.recorded: "do not take into account other aspects influencing plant survival and performance, such as snow cover, summer heat"
checks.page_wording: The USDA Hardiness Zones do not take into account other aspects influencing plant survival and performance, such as snow cover, summer heat, humidity, soil moisture, spring frosts, etc.
checks.note: US, no place stated. The full sentence names snow cover, summer heat and spring frosts (recorded fragment stops before spring frosts, but the page includes them). Supports the whole finding; 'winter cold only' is implied by the zone definition.

also_says.quote: The USDA Hardiness Zones do not take into account other aspects influencing plant survival and performance, such as snow cover, summer heat, humidity, soil moisture, spring frosts, etc.
also_says.note: Page limits zones to winter minimum temperature; no timing of rose tasks given; US, no place stated.

checks.recorded: "The most northern zone (5a) is isolated to the very northwest corner of the state"
checks.page_wording: The most northern zone (5a) is isolated to the very northwest corner of the state.
checks.note: Sentence is about Illinois (state climatologist, Illinois) and where zone 5a lies; it says nothing about rose timing, months, or whether rose sources use zones. Page says Illinois spans zones 5a to 7b, which at most shows one state holds several zones; it does not support the finding.

checks.recorded: "In the Willamette Valley, prune from mid-February to early March"
checks.page_wording: In the Willamette Valley, prune from mid-February to early March, when the weather is conducive for the plants to start growing.
checks.note: Oregon State Extension, Willamette Valley, Oregon: spring pruning of established roses mid-February to early March. It supports a mid-February to early March window for that valley only; it is not among the December or mid-April examples in the finding (a different state/area from the ones named).

contradictions: Page warns that earlier pruning (before the last hard frost or forecasted cold weather) may cause die-back needing repruning, so the weather qualifies the dates.

also_says.quote: Earlier pruning (before the last hard frost or forecasted cold weather) may cause die-back that necessitates repruning.
also_says.note: Spring pruning, Willamette Valley, Oregon; a frost/weather condition on the mid-February to early March window.

also_says.quote: The oil needs to be applied before the rose sends out new shoots.
also_says.note: Dormant oil spray (type: horticultural/dormant oil), applied after pruning and before new shoots; Willamette Valley, Oregon; no month.
